title: What is Best Practice for Training Intensity and Duration Distribution in Endurance Athletes?
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: Nationally and internationally competitive endurance athletes training 10 to 13 times a week (descriptive studies), and already well-trained athletes (intensification studies); the abstract names no sport or sample size
findings: Descriptive studies of nationally or internationally competitive endurance athletes who train 10 to 13 times a week seem to converge on a typical intensity distribution in which about 80% of training sessions are performed at low intensity (2 mM blood lactate), with about 20% dominated by periods of high-intensity work, such as intervals at about 90% VO2max.
Endurance athletes appear to self-organize toward a high-volume training approach with careful application of high-intensity training incorporated throughout the training cycle.

Training intensification studies in already well-trained athletes do not give convincing evidence that a greater emphasis on high-intensity interval training brings long-term performance gains in that population.

The author concludes that a predominance of low-intensity, long-duration training combined with fewer, highly intensive bouts may be complementary for adaptive signalling and technical mastery at an acceptable level of stress.
limitations: Only the abstract was read: the full text is closed access (OpenAlex lists no open copy on 2026-10-31) and the athletes, studies and numbers behind the pattern are unknown here. A narrative review that describes what competitive athletes seem to do, not what works. The 80/20 split is a share of sessions, not of time, in athletes who train 10 to 13 times a week, so it is neither a time share (E4 counts time) nor a prescription for recreational runners. The author co-wrote the 2022 invited commentary 'Polarized Training Is Optimal for Endurance Athletes' (authors read on Crossref), so the paper comes from an advocate of the polarized pattern; the abstract states no conflict.
implications: Cite it only for the description that most sessions of competitive endurance athletes are easy and a minority are hard. It does not support a time share, a recreational runner's plan or a choice between polarized and pyramidal.
No rule, Param or preset cites it for a number. Where a rule needs the low-intensity floor, its grade comes from the papers that count time (E4).

r3.note: Published September 2010 and not corrected. Later corpus papers describe the same low-intensity dominance by time and qualify it for runners: sperlich-2023-tid-phases, haugen-2022-world-class-runners and casado-2022-elite-runners-review (elite runners mostly pyramidal). The description stands; the 2025 network meta-analysis (rosenblat-2025-tid-ipd-nma) finds no performance difference between polarized and pyramidal.

r4.note: For the description only: sperlich-2023-tid-phases (more than 80% in zone 1 with under 12% in zone 2 in running) is by a different group and agrees on low-intensity dominance. haugen-2022-world-class-runners agrees too, but Seiler co-wrote it, so it counts as the same group. No source read tests the 80/20 split for performance.

r5.note: The population is competitive athletes training 10 to 13 times a week, across endurance sports. Use for a recreational runner of 3 to 5 runs a week is extrapolated, and the record limits its implications to a description.

r6.note: A journal paper keeps the level of its design (a narrative review, level D); the caps by class are for sources outside the journals.
